introduction: “By ‘arts and sciences’ is meant those which begin with words and end with words.” Bahá’u’lláh praised knowledge as wings for the soul and, in the same tablets, condemned a kind of learning that bears no fruit. These hundred quotations follow that criticism through its targets: the scholar who makes a show of humility or of knowledge; the seminary curriculum of nineteenth-century Persia, where years went to hair-splitting; philosophy that is conjecture; superstition; mystics who mistake their own imaginings for inner reality, and ascetics who torment the body; worship that has become form or entertainment; and, most often, the learned of each age who failed to recognize the Messenger when the unlettered did. Several passages are sharp words about particular traditions, spoken in particular settings; they should be read as that, and Chaucer’s Parson and Hosea’s “destroyed for lack of knowledge” are placed here as reminders of the other side. The prophets and the Gospels are the readings’ nearest kin. Bacon’s “cobwebs of learning,” Sa‘dí’s bee without honey, the Dhammapada’s cowherd, the Qur’án’s ass carrying books, Khayyám, Emerson and Thoreau make the same complaint in other schools. Aristotle and Proverbs speak for knowledge sought for its own sake.
questions: “Such arts and sciences … as are productive of good results.” By this test, which of your own studies have borne fruit, and which began and ended in words?
Aristotle held that the desire to know needs no justification. Is there a conflict between his view and Bahá’u’lláh’s? How would you settle the case of knowledge with no foreseeable use?
“He who tendeth sheep” may be superior to one who has read every book. What exactly gives him the advantage? Is it ignorance?
Several readings criticize mystics and ascetics. What do they affirm about the inner life while rejecting these excesses?
The harshest passages speak of the clergy and scholars of particular times and places. How should a reader today apply them without contempt for the learned or for other faiths?
“People know of Jesus Christ His name … utterly unaware of the use of the lamp.” Of which names that you repeat might the same be said?

outside.why: One sits “amid the sandals by the door whilst coveting in his heart the seat of honour.” Jesus on the opposite manoeuvre with the same motive: they love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues.
His advice: when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room. The reading shows how even that can be turned into display.
“Who wouldst appear as other than thou art?” Richard III admires his own technique: and seem a saint, when most I play the devil.
People know the name of the Lamp and repeat it, “unaware … that it should give light.” Jesus: not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven.

Sciences that “begin with words and end with words.” Bacon said it of the schoolmen in the same year-span: the mind working upon itself, as the spider worketh his web, brings forth cobwebs of learning, admirable for the fineness of thread and work, but of no substance or profit.

Aristotle begins his Metaphysics by praising knowledge that has no use: all men by nature desire to know. Is curiosity for its own sake among the “words” the reading rejects? What would Bahá’u’lláh’s test, fruit and the well-being of people, say about pure mathematics or astronomy?
The learned should direct people to knowledge “of use.” James: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
“Academic pursuits” that end in words. Ecclesiastes: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.

When Bahá’ís repeat the Greatest Name they “visualize … the divine characteristics” and try to live them. Marcus Aurelius: no longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
Thanksgiving said “with the lips merely.” Claudius at prayer: my words fly up, my thoughts remain below: words without thoughts never to heaven go.
Without virtues, “the mere acquisition of learning and arts will not suffice.” Paul: though I understand all mysteries, and all knowledge, and have not charity, I am nothing.
“With learning cometh arrogance and pride.” Paul: knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.

“A mere drop will perhaps shut a man off from flooding grace.” Proverbs has no such hesitation: wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom. When does learning lead to its Object, on the reading’s account, and when does it bar the way?

The ignorant man adorned with knowledge “forbids the helpless servants from that which benefits them.” Jesus: ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.
Intelligent people see customs contrary to reason and “forsake the divine religion.” Lucretius is the classic case: ’tis that same religion oftener far hath bred the foul impieties of men.
Students waste years on “material that is pure supposition.” Paul: neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying.
Hair-splitting spent on trifles. Jesus: ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith.
All are commanded “not to pursue matters that do not yield” results. The Buddha’s parable of the man shot with an arrow who will not have it drawn until he knows the archer’s name, clan and village.
Futile disciplines “cause confusion … One should not waste time on them.” Paul: avoid foolish questions, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
Sciences that “were mere imaginations, but their names were great.” Paul: avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called.
Students who “spend all their lives in that institution with no visible result.” Paul: ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá contrasts them with the Western college that turns out engineers. Emerson found the same fault in Western colleges: meek young men grow up in libraries, believing it their duty to accept the views which Cicero, which Locke, which Bacon, have given. Is the failing a matter of subject, or of the student’s relation to what he studies?

Philosophers who “start in word and end in word.” Omar Khayyám: myself when young did eagerly frequent Doctor and Saint, and heard great argument about it and about: but evermore came out by the same door where in I went.
A poet’s book of many years is found to be “like the cobweb.” Sa‘dí: one being asked what a learned man without practice resembled, replied: A bee without honey.
Free thought from fetters laid on it “without proof or evidence,” like the theories of Ptolemy. Whitman, tired of charts, went out and looked up in perfect silence at the stars.
Socrates on the first step out of inherited error: he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know.
“God hath made conjecture … a manifest sin.” The Qur’án: they follow but a guess, and lo! a guess can never take the place of the truth.
Tear their cobwebs and they spin again. Jeremiah: can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?
“What captives of superstitions people are!” Bacon: in all superstition wise men follow fools.
Old superstitions should not be spread in a gathering meant for truth. Bacon: it were better to have no opinion of God at all, than such an opinion as is unworthy of him.
The bee builds its comb with precision and needs no teacher. Proverbs sends the idle to another small creature: go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.
Those who worship “the idol which their imaginations have carved, and who call it Inner Reality.” The psalm on idols: they have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not.
Xenophanes on where such idols come from: horses would paint the forms of the gods like horses, and oxen like oxen.

Whoever worships the conception in his own mind “is worshipping the product of his imagination.” Feuerbach held that all worship is this and nothing more: the true sense of Theology is Anthropology. Where do the readings agree with him, and at what point do they part?

The Sufi doctrine that the creature can lose itself in the attributes of God, as iron in fire. Plotinus taught the inward way that lies behind it: withdraw into yourself and look. What is the difference between purifying the mirror, which the readings ask, and becoming the sun?

Tales of the spirit leaving the body are told with a smile. Paul reports one of his own, and with great reserve: whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth. What does Paul’s reticence share with the readings’ scepticism?
Imagined journeys in the sky were “the cause of their downfall.” Paul warns against one intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind.

A devotee struck himself against stone and wall for four hours. The prophets of Baal: they cried aloud, and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets; and there was neither voice, nor any to answer.
Some claim they would cast themselves into the fire. “Cast thyself into the light.” Paul: though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.
Ascetics who deny themselves food and live with wild beasts. The Buddha had tried it for six years: avoiding both of these extremes, the middle way.
“Many worshippers and countless ascetics, yet few are truly wakeful.” Isaiah: is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, and to let the oppressed go free.
The Qur’án on Christian asceticism: monasticism they invented; We ordained it not for them.
They followed the path for years, awaiting the dawn, and missed it. Jesus to the students of scripture: search the scriptures; they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me.

Those who “considered themselves discoverers of mysteries” have grown cold. Isaiah: the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed; the learned saith, I cannot; for it is sealed.
Dervishes who claim maturity and mystical knowledge. The Tao Te Ching: he who knows does not speak about it; he who is ever ready to speak about it does not know it.
A gathering whose only fruit was “the spread of superstitions.” Paul: beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men.

Religious leaders think religion lies “in the adherence to a collection of certain dogmas and the practice of rites.” Hosea: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
Micah: what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
“Some priests are in holy office for no other reason than to gain their living.” Milton: blind mouths! that scarce themselves know how to hold a sheep-hook. The hungry sheep look up, and are not fed.

Chaucer, who satirized such clergy, also drew the other kind, and he belongs beside the readings’ severity: this noble ensample to his sheep he yaf, that first he wroghte, and afterward he taughte. What would make a reader of these passages unjust to the Parson?

Places of worship “have become gathering-places of entertainment.” Ezekiel was told the same of his own congregation: thou art unto them as a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice; for they hear thy words, but they do them not.
Amos: I hate, I despise your feast days. Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs.
Worship associated with “amusements and pastimes.” Jesus in the Temple: make not my Father’s house an house of merchandise.
A man who has done every wrong asks whether God’s government is so childlike as to forgive it all for a word. Paul: shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.
A learned man who claimed to comprehend the teachings flew into a rage when tested. Proverbs: seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him.
He judged a shopkeeper dissolute by what he saw. Jesus: judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
“Be thou of the people of hell-fire, but be not a hypocrite.” The letter to Laodicea: I would thou wert cold or hot.
“Make thy home in taverns, but tread not the path of the mischief-maker.” Jesus to the respectable: the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.
The reading quotes the Qur’án: as for poets, the erring follow them.

Socrates examined the poets and found: not by wisdom do poets write poetry, but by a sort of genius and inspiration; they say many fine things, but do not understand the meaning of them. The reading goes on to praise a poet who speaks truth. What separates the two kinds?
They “mumble about sciences” like parrots. The Qur’án: the likeness of those who are entrusted with the Law, yet apply it not, is as the likeness of the ass carrying books.
The Dhammapada: the thoughtless man, even if he can recite a large portion of the law, but is not a doer of it, is like a cowherd counting the cows of others.
A hundred thousand guides “wandering in the valley of error while claiming to show the way.” Jesus: they be blind leaders of the blind.
The reading uses the Gospel’s words: beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
Divines who “do not accept one another, each counting himself to be the most accomplished and most pious.” The Pharisee: God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are.
Souls “confused by the fabricated traditions of the foolish.” Jesus: making the word of God of none effect through your tradition.
“Preoccupation with tales and stories” that cast doubt into weak hearts. Paul: they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.
Scholars “have drawn from turbid springs.” Jeremiah: they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living waters.
A sifter of wheat recognized what the learned denied. Paul: not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called.
The council, of two fishermen: they perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, and they marvelled.
“Though outwardly thou art not among the learned,” thou hast attained. The crowd, of Jesus: how knoweth this man letters, having never learned?
A scholar who “carried volumes of books” and did not attain. Paul: professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.
He fled, “for it is indeed difficult for him to lay down his burden.” The rich young man, of another kind of wealth: he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions.

“He who tendeth sheep in the valleys” may be superior to those who have read all the books. Amos to the priest of Bethel: I was no prophet; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: and the Lord took me as I followed the flock.
Hosea gives the warning on the other side: my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Does the reading put ignorance above learning? What is it that the shepherd has and the reader lacks?
“He is truly learned who hath acknowledged My Revelation.” Jeremiah: let not the wise man glory in his wisdom; but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me.
“Those whom knowledge hath prevented from the Known One.” Paul: where is the wise? where is the scribe? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
“Beware lest learning debar you.” Jesus: thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
“Follow not every veiled learned one.” Jesus: do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not.
Men of learning who are “worshippers of vain imaginings.” Jeremiah: how do ye say, We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us? Lo, the pen of the scribes is in vain.
Divines as “the fountainhead of vain imaginings.” Paul: thou art confident that thou thyself art a guide of the blind; thou therefore which teachest another, teachest thou not thyself?
“Blessed is the learned one who beholdeth the Truth with his own eyes.” The Qur’án honours such learning: are those who know equal with those who know not?
The psalmist: I have more understanding than all my teachers: for thy testimonies are my meditation.
“How many a worshipper hath worshipped God through nights and days, yet … denied Him.” Isaiah: with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me.
Mystics who claimed knowledge “turned away when He Who conversed with God” appeared. Jesus: had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me.
Worship as countless as the sands, with heedlessness of the Cause, is idolatry. Amos: take thou away from me the noise of thy songs. But let judgment run down as waters.

People drown in hopes, imaginings, desire, and “in knowledge.” Thomas à Kempis: what will it avail thee to engage in reasonings concerning the Trinity, if thou be void of humility? I had rather feel compunction, than know the definition of it.

A pity that one with insight should seek light “from the moon of imagination which is in eclipse.” Wordsworth: one impulse from a vernal wood may teach you more of man, of moral evil and of good, than all the sages can.
They “seek after thorns and thistles … clinging instead to pebbles.” Isaiah: wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not?
“Shatter the idols of vain imaginings.” Paul: ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God.
Those who follow imaginings “are in doubt and hypocrisy.” The Qur’án: O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not?
“The sun of idle fancies hath been eclipsed … this is the day of divine disclosure.” Paul: now it is high time to awake out of sleep.
The conjectures of those “whom God hath made worse than cattle.” The phrase is the Qur’án’s: having hearts wherewith they understand not; these are as the cattle—nay, but they are worse.
Bahá’u’lláh says He has long been disinclined to “scholarly investigation.” Paul: my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit.
A plain letter in Persian is “more beloved before God than the utterances of the deluded.” Jesus weighed two mites the same way: this poor widow hath cast in more than they all.
Some “cling to words while turning away from the Munificent One.” Thoreau: there are nowadays professors of philosophy, but not philosophers.
Others “grasp at learning while remaining heedless.” Confucius: learning without thought is labor lost; thought without learning is perilous.
“The veil of pride has prevented eyes from beholding the lights, and their hearts are sealed.” Isaiah: make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes.
“The brilliant lamp gloweth within the delicate glass.” Jesus: neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick.

A blessing on those who have “cast aside vain imaginings.” The Qur’án’s question to the learned of every faith: enjoin ye righteousness upon mankind while ye yourselves forget to practise it? And ye are readers of the Scripture!

quran-they-follow-but-a-guess.text: And they have no knowledge thereof. They follow but a guess, and lo! a guess can never take the place of the truth.

kings-cut-themselves-after-their-manner.text: And they cried aloud, and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them. And it came to pass, when midday was past, and they prophesied until the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, that there was neither voice, nor any to answer, nor any that regarded

john-house-of-merchandise.text: And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise

psalm-more-understanding-than-all-my-tea.text: I have more understanding than all my teachers: for thy testimonies are my meditation. I understand more than the ancients, because I keep thy precepts

romans-professing-themselves-to-be-wise.text: Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools

bacon-cobwebs-of-learning.text: but if it work upon itself, as the spider worketh his web, then it is endless, and brings forth indeed cobwebs of learning, admirable for the fineness of thread and work, but of no substance or profit
bacon-cobwebs-of-learning.author: Francis Bacon

kempis-reasonings-concerning-the-trinity.text: What will it avail thee to engage in reasonings concerning the Trinity, if thou be void of humility, and art therefore displeasing to the Trinity? Surely great words do not make a man holy and just; but a virtuous life maketh him dear to God. I had rather feel compunction, than know the definition of it
kempis-reasonings-concerning-the-trinity.author: Thomas à Kempis

dhammapada-cowherd-counting-the-cows-of-.text: The thoughtless man, even if he can recite a large portion (of the law), but is not a doer of it, has no share in the priesthood, but is like a cowherd counting the cows of others

saadi-bee-without-honey.text: One being asked what a learned man without practice resembled, replied: 'A bee without honey
saadi-bee-without-honey.author: Saʿdī

khayyam-came-out-by-the-same-door.text: Myself when young did eagerly frequent / Doctor and Saint, and heard great argument / About it and about: but evermore / Came out by the same door where in I went
khayyam-came-out-by-the-same-door.author: Omar Khayyám
khayyam-came-out-by-the-same-door.locator: quatrain 27 in Edward FitzGerald’s fifth edition

emerson-meek-young-men-in-libraries.text: Meek young men grow up in libraries, believing it their duty to accept the views, which Cicero, which Locke, which Bacon, have given, forgetful that Cicero, Locke, and Bacon were only young men in libraries when they wrote these books
emerson-meek-young-men-in-libraries.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

plato-i-neither-know-nor-think-that-i-kn.text: I am better off than he is - for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know
plato-i-neither-know-nor-think-that-i-kn.author: Plato

thoreau-professors-of-philosophy.text: There are nowadays professors of philosophy, but not philosophers. Yet it is admirable to profess because it was once admirable to live
thoreau-professors-of-philosophy.author: Henry David Thoreau
